target.name: ByteCodeInterpreter object append (sub_0801191A)
target.role: append a value to the array carried by the object at 0x03001C4C
target.notes: sub_0801191A, 18 bytes and 9 instructions, one terminator at 0x0801192A, NO calls and NO literal pool. A LEAF, so the effect is established by this routine alone. THE CONCRETE EFFECT: it APPENDS the incoming value at index `count` of an array carried by the object, then increments that count. The object holds a 32-bit COUNT at +0x04 and an array of 32-bit values beginning at +0x08, so `sub_0801191A(object, value)` performs `((u32*)object)[1] += 1` and `*(u32*)(object + 8 + 4*count) = value`, where count is the value READ BEFORE the increment, so element `count` is written and not element `count+1`. OBJECT-RELATIVE ACCESSES, ALL OF THEM: +0x04 is read and then written 32-bit as the count; +0x08 + 4*count is written 32-bit as the appended element; and +0x00 IS NOT TOUCHED at all, neither read nor written. There is no other access in the routine. ORDER: the count is loaded first, stored back incremented second, and only then is the element written; both complete before the routine returns and nothing interrupts them. THERE IS NO CAPACITY CHECK: nothing compares the count against a limit and no capacity is reachable from this routine, so a large count writes far past any sane array end - the machine's behaviour, reproduced rather than guarded. THE RETURN VALUE IS NOT DEFINED: the routine ends with `bx lr` with r0 holding the address of the element it just wrote, not a status and not a boolean, so the reconstruction returns void rather than inventing a result. THE INCOMING CONTRACT, re-proven from the caller: native dispatch slot 178 at 0x08003030 calls this with r0 = *(0x08054FBC + 0x18), which the static layout resolves to the IWRAM object 0x03001C4C, and r1 = the value returned by sub_0802BFBC. THE FIRST CONCRETE EFFECT OF THE WHOLE CHAIN: slot 178 pops three VM values, computes one from them, and hands it here, where it is APPENDED to the object's array. So the object is a growable-by-write collection rather than a scalar and the handler is a producer for it. This object is the most heavily referenced entry in the static pointer table, so its count-and-array shape is recorded for reuse. UNKNOWN: what the object is, what its +0x00 field means, what the appended values are used for, who reads them, and whether a capacity limit exists elsewhere. No semantic name is assigned to the object, the array or the count, and nothing is imported from another title.
